title: Renting in Germany: house rules, tenant rights and regional differences
description: What tenants can expect in Germany: quiet hours, deposits, notice periods, the rights German law gives you and how rents differ between regions.
html:
Germany is a country of renters; more than half of households rent rather than own, and the law reflects that with strong protections for tenants. It also comes with customs that newcomers do not always expect. Here is what to know before you sign.

City and countryside

Rents in Munich, Frankfurt, Hamburg, Stuttgart and Berlin are two to three times what you pay in a mid-sized town. The gap has widened in the last decade. If your job or university allows it, a town 30 minutes from a big city often halves the rent for the same space.

Regional differences

Southern Germany is the most expensive, the east outside Berlin and Leipzig the cheapest. Flats in the west tend to come without a fitted kitchen; in the east, kitchens are more often included. Some cities apply a rent cap that limits how far a new rent may exceed the local average.

House rules

Quiet hours (Ruhezeiten) run from 10 pm to 6 am and often over lunchtime and all day Sunday: no drilling, loud music or vacuuming. Waste is separated into several bins, and your neighbours will notice if you get it wrong. Many buildings rotate stairwell cleaning between tenants. None of this is enforced by law, but it is enforced by neighbours.

Your rights

A deposit is capped at three months' base rent and must be held in a separate account. Unlimited contracts are the norm and the landlord can only terminate for specific reasons, such as needing the flat for their own family. Rent increases are limited in size and frequency. Repairs to the structure are the landlord's responsibility; the contract usually makes minor repairs and cosmetic maintenance yours. The tenant's notice period is three months.

Before you sign

Read the contract for the service charges (Nebenkosten), which are billed annually and can produce a surprise bill. Take dated photos of the flat at handover and get a signed handover protocol. Register your address within two weeks of moving in; you will need the landlord's confirmation for that. And join a tenants' association if you expect a dispute; membership costs little and includes legal advice.
